blocks.text: A range of disorders can affect the respiratory system and interfere with respiration, from mild and self-limiting conditions such as the common cold to more severe diseases such as sinusitis, otitis media, pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis, emphysema and COPD.
Upper respiratory tract infections
Upper respiratory tract infections (URIs) affect the nose, throat, sinuses and larynx and can be easily transmitted from person to person through respiratory droplets.
Sinusitis

Sinusitis is the inflammation of the lining of the sinuses, four paired air-filled spaces that surround the nasal cavity: under the eyes, above the eyes, between the eyes and behind the eyes. It may be acute, lasting 7 to 10 days, or chronic, lasting longer than 12 weeks. Most cases are due to viral infections; some are bacterial and rare cases involve fungal infections. Its symptoms include fever, a plugged nose, pus-like nasal discharge, loss of the sense of smell, facial pain, a feeling that phlegm is falling from the back of the nose into the throat, and a headache that is sometimes aggravated by bending over. Most cases are caused by viruses and resolve without antibiotics; if the infection is bacterial, antibiotics or sulpha drugs are usually prescribed, and the physician may also prescribe nebulisation to reduce the inflammation in the sinuses and nose and speed recovery. For chronic or recurring sinusitis, treatment may include nasal surgery in which the pathogens and mucus are removed.

blocks.text: Otitis media

Otitis media is the inflammation of the middle ear. It may be acute (rapid onset) or chronic (lasting more than six weeks). The common cause is the accumulation of fluid in the Eustachian tube that cannot be drained from the middle ear; the undrained fluid allows bacteria and viruses to grow in the middle ear. Symptoms include severe ear pain, pulling at one or both ears, fever, fluid draining from the ear, loss of balance and hearing difficulties. Treatments include oral and topical pain killers and antibiotics if the cause is bacterial.

The Eustachian tube runs down from the middle ear and is narrowed.

blocks.text: Lower respiratory tract infections
Lower respiratory tract infections include pneumonia, pulmonary tuberculosis, lung abscess and bronchitis.
Pneumonia

Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that can cause mild to life-threatening illness. In pneumonia the alveoli of one or both lungs are inflamed and filled with pus and fluid, which makes breathing painful and limits oxygen intake. It is most commonly caused by viruses or bacteria and is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide. A variety of organisms can cause it, primarily bacteria (particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae) or viruses (such as human rhinovirus) and less commonly fungi. Its symptoms include cough with phlegm, shortness of breath, chest pain, fever, blueness of the skin, loss of appetite, a high heart rate and fatigue. Specific antibiotics treat bacterial pneumonia, analgesics reduce fever and pain, and vaccination prevents certain bacterial and viral pneumonias in children and adults.

blocks.alt: A lung whose lower part is darkened where pneumonia affects it. Two enlarged boxes: normal alveoli, thin-walled and empty; and alveoli with pneumonia, with thick inflamed walls and filled with pus and fluid.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.12: Pneumonia (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.12).

blocks.title: Pneumonia in children
blocks.text: Pneumonia killed more than 808,000 children under the age of five in 2017, accounting for 15% of all deaths of children under five.
Pulmonary tuberculosis

Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic infection caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It can affect many parts of the body but generally affects the lungs; tuberculosis of the lungs is pulmonary tuberculosis. It is highly contagious and spreads through coughs or sneezes. The bacteria enter the lungs, multiply, and cause inflammation and damage to the lung tissue, including the alveoli; the damage can form small cavities or holes in the lung tissue, which makes it difficult for the lungs to function properly. In advanced stages the alveoli are so damaged that the lungs may be unable to supply the body with enough oxygen, leading to respiratory failure, a medical emergency. The major symptoms are cough with blood, intermittent fever usually in the evening, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, depression, weakness and dry cough, and chest pain due to inflammation of the pleura. Treatment uses multiple antibiotics taken regularly over a long period of months.

blocks.alt: The trachea and both lungs; the upper part of the left lung (right of the picture) has several dark holes, the cavities made by tuberculosis.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.13: A lung affected with TB (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.13).

blocks.text: Disorders of the lungs
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

COPD is a chronic inflammatory disease of the lungs. Its common causes are tobacco smoking and long-term exposure to harmful pollutants and chemical fumes; a small percentage of people with a genetic predisposition (deficiency of the protein alpha-1 antitrypsin) can also develop COPD without smoking or significant exposure to pollutants. The symptoms are a persistent cough with mucus (sputum), shortness of breath, wheezing, chest tightness, fatigue and frequent respiratory tract infections. COPD is incurable, but minimising exposure to smoke, pollutants and chemicals slows its progression; other therapies are bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen therapy, and in some severe cases surgery such as lung transplantation may be considered.

blocks.alt: Small lungs with a boxed area enlarged below: a bronchiole cut across shows a thickened, inflamed lining and mucus filling its narrowed lumen; at its end, enlarged blocked alveoli hold trapped air.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.14: A lung affected by COPD (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.14).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Mucus, Inflamed lining of bronchiole, Trapped air, Enlarged blocked alveoli.

blocks.text: Emphysema

Emphysema is a type of COPD in which the inner walls of the alveoli are damaged and eventually rupture, creating one larger air space instead of many small ones and reducing the surface area available for gas exchange. Its primary cause is smoking; it can also be caused by long-term exposure to air pollution, dust or chemical fumes, or by a genetic deficiency of the protein alpha-1 antitrypsin. Its symptoms are shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, fatigue and chest tightness. Quitting smoking is the most important step in managing it, as continued smoking speeds the progression of the disease; other treatments are bronchodilators, inhaled steroids, oxygen therapy and pulmonary rehabilitation.

blocks.alt: A lung with two areas enlarged in boxes: normal alveoli, many small sacs in grape-like clusters; and damaged alveoli, a few large air spaces whose inner walls have broken down.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.15: Emphysema (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.15).

blocks.title: Chronic bronchitis
blocks.text: Chronic bronchitis is another type of COPD, involving inflammation and narrowing of the bronchial tubes with increased mucus production that further blocks the airways and makes breathing difficult; it lasts from three months to two years. It is caused by long-term exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution or industrial dusts, and its symptoms are almost the same as COPD: wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness and frequent respiratory infections. It is managed by quitting smoking, with bronchodilators, pulmonary rehabilitation and in some cases oxygen therapy.
